Aspirin and other NSAIDs, or paracetamol are often tried first for the symptomatic treatment of vari- ous types of headache including migraine (p.616) and tension-type headache (p.617). NSAIDs may also be effective for the prophylaxis of migraine, although they are not considered first-line options. Opioid analgesics such as codeine are sometimes included in oral compound analgesic preparations used in the initial treatment of migraine or tension-type headache, but are best avoided, especially in patients who have frequent at- tacks. Labour pain. It is important to assess the adverse effects, on both the mother and the fetus, when selecting any meth- od for the management of labour pain. Non-pharmacolog- ical methods of pain relief may include relaxation tech- niques, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (which is popular with patients, although there is no robust evi- dence of benefit1), and various other complementary ther- apies: of the latter, there is some evidence of benefit with the use of acupuncture and hypnosis.2 Water immersion (use of a birthing pool) during the first stage of labour has been shown to reduce reported maternal pain.3 Subcutane- ous or intradermal injection of sterile water into the back has also been used for the relief of low back pain during labour.4,5 However, at some point during labour many women will request some sort of pharmacological analgesia. The inhalational anaesthetic nitrous oxide, given with oxy- gen, is suitable for self-administration and is commonly used to relieve labour pain. It is relatively safe and can pro- duce substantial analgesia in most patients.6 Other inhala- tional analgesics such as isoflurane or sevoflurane are also sometimes used7 (see Choice of Analgesic, above).
